title: Regulatory & Permitting Map (The Gating System)
summary: This is the module to overlearn. Every construction activity on Solara Shores is gated by an approval, and the marine approvals are the long poles. Three chains run in parallel: the land-side chain (planning → building permits → inspections → occupancy), the environmental chain (EIA → CEC, which gates EVERYTHING), and the commercial chain (licences, VAT, NIB, work permits).

sections.heading: The land-side chain
sections.body: 1) Subdivision/planning approval from the Department of Physical Planning / Town Planning Committee — zoning conformity, subdivision layout, land use; larger schemes can involve public notice and hearings. 2) Building permits from the Ministry of Works (MOW), Buildings Control Division — applications route in parallel to the Civil Design Section (drainage, road access), Physical Planning (zoning), Environmental Health, then MOW's own structural/mechanical/electrical/plumbing checks. Drawings must be signed by a Bahamas-registered architect and a registered professional engineer (Professional Engineers Act 2004 — foreign engineers need temporary registration and association with a Bahamian PE). Nominal processing is 6–8 weeks per permit after COMPLETE submission; longer when external agencies weigh in. Permits are valid 18 months, extendable. For 302 homes you run a permit PIPELINE, not a permit — batch submissions by phase and track them like a production schedule. 3) Inspections through construction (setback, foundation/rebar, slab, frame/block, electrical rough, plumbing rough, final), then the Occupancy Certificate per building. The OC is what allows closings — OC throughput is a revenue gate, not a paperwork detail.

sections.heading: The environmental chain — the project's master gate
sections.body: The Department of Environmental Planning and Protection (DEPP) administers the Environmental Planning and Protection Act 2019 and the EIA Regulations 2020 (amended 2026). A project of this class requires: preliminary review → a full EIA by a DEPP-pre-approved consultant → published notice → MANDATORY public consultation → an Environmental Management Plan (EMP) → a Certificate of Environmental Clearance (CEC) before commencement. Land clearing IS commencement — nothing physical happens before the CEC. DEPP can require an environmental performance bond of up to 5% of project value, continues oversight through construction, and can stop work for EMP non-compliance. The EMP's conditions — turbidity limits, seasonal work windows, monitoring reports — become enforceable constraints on your dredging and beach contractors: write them into the subcontracts verbatim. Realistic duration for a marine-inclusive EIA: 6–14 months. This is why the environmental workstream starts before everything else — it is the critical path's critical path.

sections.heading: The seabed: Crown property, lease only
sections.body: Groins, marina structures, jetties, moorings — anything on the seabed — now requires a formal seabed lease from the Port Department under the Port Authorities (Amendment) Act 2025. The seabed is Crown property; policy is lease-only, never sale. Applications need site plans, financials, and supporting permits. Port Department approval letters are also a listed prerequisite for MOW building permits on docks and marine structures — the agencies cross-reference each other, so sequence the applications deliberately.

sections.heading: The commercial chain
sections.body: Business Licence (Department of Inland Revenue) for the development entities AND every subcontractor — verify each sub holds one, because unlicensed subs are a compliance exposure to you. VAT registration. NIB registration as an employer. Work permits via the Department of Immigration for any non-Bahamian labor or specialists: the labour-market test requires a certified vacancy showing no Bahamian is available; long-term permits renew annually; under-90-day short-term permits cover visiting specialists like dredge crews. Processing runs 4–8+ weeks per foreign specialist. If foreign investment structure is involved, Bahamas Investment Authority / NEC approval and International Persons Landholding Act compliance sit upstream of everything. Finally, concessions: large developments negotiate duty concessions via a Heads of Agreement with government — an owner-level negotiation, but the CM must know exactly what is and isn't covered, because it changes every purchase order.

quiz.teach: The Certificate of Environmental Clearance (CEC) must be issued before 'commencement' of the project — and the definition of commencement is broader than most developers assume.
quiz.prompt: The EIA is in public consultation and going well. Your earthworks contractor has idle machines and offers a discount to start land clearing now. Legal?

choices.text: No — clearing is commencement, and commencement before the CEC is prohibited
choices.why: Correct. Land clearing is physical commencement. Starting before the CEC risks stop-work, enforcement, and poisoning your relationship with DEPP for the whole project.

choices.text: Yes, as long as you stay 100 ft from the shoreline
choices.why: There is no shoreline-buffer exemption — the CEC gates ALL physical work, upland included.
Clearing IS commencement under the environmental framework. This is exactly the trap the discount is inviting you into.

choices.text: Yes, if the contractor accepts the risk in writing
choices.why: The CEC obligation runs to the project and its owner. A contractor's risk acceptance letter does not transfer regulatory exposure — DEPP stops YOUR project.

quiz.explanation: Nothing physical happens before the CEC — this is the sim's hardest gate. A discount on clearing is trivial against a DEPP stop-work order, a damaged regulator relationship, and possible conditions added to your CEC. The correct use of the waiting period is paper: permits, procurement, agreements.

quiz.teach: The Occupancy Certificate (OC) is issued per building after final inspections pass.
quiz.prompt: Why is OC throughput described as 'a revenue gate, not a paperwork detail'?

choices.text: Because unit closings — the project's revenue — cannot happen until each building has its OC
choices.why: Correct. A finished house with no OC is inventory you cannot convert to cash. The OC-to-closing lag runs 2–6 weeks even when everything goes right.

choices.text: Because the OC triggers the final construction draw
choices.why: Draws track construction progress; the OC's real teeth are on the sales side — no OC, no closing, no revenue.

choices.text: Because insurance rates drop once the OC issues
choices.why: Occupied-building insurance does differ, but the reason the OC is a REVENUE gate is that closings legally require it.

choices.text: Because the HOA can't form without OCs
choices.why: The condo legal structure is established in step with construction — the OC's direct bite is that buyers cannot close without it.

quiz.explanation: The whole production machine — inspections passed in sequence, punch complete, OC issued, closing scheduled — is the pipeline that turns construction spend back into cash. A CM who treats final inspections casually is choking the project's revenue at its last step.

quiz.teach: The environmental chain has a strict internal order, and it gates all physical work.
quiz.prompt: Put the environmental approval chain in order:
items: Full EIA prepared by a DEPP-pre-approved consultant
Published notice and mandatory public consultation
quiz.explanation: Preliminary review scopes the assessment; the EIA must come from a consultant DEPP has pre-approved; the public consultation is mandatory, not optional; the EMP converts the EIA's mitigation into enforceable conditions; and only the CEC unlocks physical work. Budget 6–14 months for the chain on a marine-inclusive project.

quiz.teach: The seabed around the Bahamas is Crown property, and the Port Authorities (Amendment) Act 2025 formalized how private structures occupy it.
quiz.prompt: Which of these project elements requires a seabed lease?

choices.text: The ocean groins holding the converted beach
choices.why: Correct — groins sit on Crown seabed seaward of the high-water mark, so they need a formal lease (lease-only policy; the seabed is never sold).

choices.text: The canal bulkheads inside the property
choices.why: Canals cut into your own uplands are on your land, not Crown seabed — though they still fall under the EIA/CEC.
The beach club is an upland building — MOW permit and coastal design tier, but no seabed lease.
The WWTP is upland infrastructure — Environmental Health and MOW territory, not Port Department.

quiz.explanation: Anything on the seabed — groins, marina structures seaward of the high-water mark, jetties, moorings — requires a Port Department seabed lease. And note the cross-reference trap: Port Department approval letters are a PREREQUISITE for MOW building permits on marine structures, so sequence the applications deliberately.

quiz.teach: MOW building permit processing is nominally 6–8 weeks per permit after COMPLETE submission — and a query restarts the clock.
quiz.prompt: MOW queries a batch of 20 house permits over a drainage detail. What is the real cost of the resubmittal loop?

choices.text: Roughly 6 weeks of delay to those 20 vertical starts, which ripples into the draw schedule and every downstream trade's takt
choices.why: Correct — a query doesn't just delay paper; it delays 20 foundations, which delays 20 of everything after, and the lender's draw schedule assumed those starts.
The fee is trivial. The six-week loop on 20 houses is the real cost — measured in general conditions burn ($150–400K/month across the program) and delayed revenue.

choices.text: Nothing, because construction can start while the query is resolved
choices.why: No permit, no start. That's the entire meaning of a gating system.

choices.text: Only the first house is delayed; the rest proceed
choices.why: The query hit the whole batch — this is why batching strategy matters and why a drawing coordination review BEFORE submission pays for itself.

quiz.explanation: For 302 homes you run a permit pipeline — batched by phase, tracked like a production schedule. A coordination review before each submission (civil vs architectural vs structural conflicts) is cheap insurance against the 6-week resubmittal loop, which at program scale costs months of general conditions and delayed closings.

quiz.teach: Some regulatory work you hire out to specialists; some you must own personally because it IS the developer's job.
quiz.prompt: For each regulatory workstream, decide: subcontract to a specialist, or direct-manage it yourself?

items.why: The EIA must legally come from a DEPP-pre-approved environmental consultant — you couldn't self-perform it even if you wanted to.

items.scope: The permit pipeline tracker (batches, submission dates, query status per phase)
items.why: This is production management of approvals — it drives your start releases and draw schedule, and no consultant feels the schedule pain like you do.

items.scope: Verifying every subcontractor holds a current Business Licence
items.why: Unlicensed subs are a compliance exposure to YOU. It's a checklist item in your sub-onboarding process, not something to outsource.
Drawings must be signed by a Bahamas-registered PE — this is your structural engineer's deliverable.

items.scope: The relationship with DEPP through construction
items.why: The regulator relationship is a developer asset. Consultants attend meetings, but DEPP hears bad news from YOU first — self-reporting through an intermediary reads as hiding.

quiz.explanation: Pattern: technical deliverables requiring registration or specialty (EIA, stamped drawings) are subcontracted; anything that controls schedule, compliance exposure, or a regulator relationship stays on your desk with systems behind it.

mathVariables.note: After complete submission; queries restart the loop

mathProblems.title: Environmental performance bond
mathProblems.context: DEPP can require an environmental performance bond of up to 5% of project value — cash or bonding capacity you must arrange before commencement.

mathProblems.title: The cost of a resubmittal loop
mathProblems.context: A permit query restarts the processing clock. While the batch waits, general conditions (site staff, security, temp facilities, insurance) keep burning — that's the price of an incomplete submission.

decisionPoints.title: The cheap barge in July
decisionPoints.scenario: Your groin contractor calls: their barge spread finishes another Bahamas job in late June and they'll knock 15% off mobilization if you take it straight to your site for a July–August groin campaign. The seabed lease is in hand. The EMP has a seasonal marine work window clause you haven't re-read lately.

options.label: Decline — hold marine works for the November–May calm window and re-check the EMP's seasonal restrictions
options.outcome: You pay full mobilization later, but the groins are built in workable seas, inside the EMP window, with no named-storm exposure on a half-built rock structure. The 15% 'saving' would have been consumed by the first weather standby week.

options.label: Take it, but only after pricing the risk: confirm the EMP allows summer marine work, cap weather standby in the contract, and check named-storm insurance on the spread
options.outcome: Diligence comes back mixed: the EMP restricts turbidity-generating work in summer months, and the insurer loads the premium for peak-season marine exposure. Priced honestly, the discount disappears — you decline anyway, a week later.

options.label: Grab the discount — barges are scarce and 15% is 15%
options.outcome: August: a tropical storm forecast triggers demobilization mid-campaign. Half-placed groin stone takes wave damage; the contractor invoices standby and remobilization under a force majeure clause you never tightened; DEPP queries turbidity exceedances from storm-agitated, half-finished works. The 15% is gone several times over.

decisionPoints.debrief: Marine works are planned November–May for a reason: peak hurricane season plus probable EMP seasonal restrictions make summer marine work a risk stack, not a bargain. Cheap mobilization into the wrong window is the classic false economy — if you must consider it, price every layer of the risk explicitly, and expect that pricing to kill the deal.

decisionPoints.title: Clearing during consultation
decisionPoints.scenario: The EIA public consultation wraps next month and your environmental consultant says approval looks likely. The earthworks sub can mobilize now at a discount. Sales wants site photos showing progress. Everyone is telling you to start clearing.

options.label: Hold all physical work until the CEC is issued; use the time for permit batching, procurement, and utility agreements
options.outcome: Frustrating month, perfectly used: first house-permit batch submitted, long-lead register opened, WSC and BPL agreements progressed. When the CEC lands, you mobilize into a project that's paper-ready.

options.label: Start clearing — approval is 'likely' and the discount is real
options.outcome: DEPP issues a stop-work order: commencement before CEC is prohibited, and clearing is commencement. The consultation record now includes your violation; conditions get added to the CEC; your regulator relationship starts in a hole it never fully climbs out of.

options.label: Clear just the access corridor 'for survey purposes'
options.outcome: A neighbor photographs the machines and submits it to the public consultation. Legally it's still commencement; politically it's worse — you've handed opponents evidence that you treat conditions as suggestions.

decisionPoints.debrief: The CEC gates everything, and 'likely approval' is not approval. The pre-CEC period is when good developers win the project on paper: permits batched, long-lead items released, agency agreements signed. The discipline also has a face: this site has established communities on both flanks watching everything.
